content: Edentulism refers to the condition of being toothless to some extent, resulting from the loss of teeth. Partial edentulism occurs when some teeth are lost, while complete edentulism occurs when all teeth are lost. Even organisms that naturally lack teeth, such as anteaters, sloths, and armadillos, can be described as edentulous. These animals, classified under the former zoological order Edentata, lack anterior teeth and have either no or poorly developed posterior teeth. Teeth play a critical role in human function and aesthetics. They provide structural support to the lips and cheeks, contributing to a fuller and more aesthetically pleasing facial appearance. Teeth also maintain the vertical dimension of occlusion, which is the proper alignment and spacing of the jaws. Along with the tongue and lips, teeth are essential for the correct pronunciation of various sounds. Additionally, they preserve the height of the alveolar ridge and are vital for cutting, grinding, and chewing food. When the mouth is at rest, the teeth in the upper and lower jaws are nearly touching, separated by a small freeway space of about 2-3 mm. This space is maintained by the teeth preventing further closure beyond the point of maximum intercuspation. In the absence of teeth, the natural vertical dimension of occlusion is lost, and the mouth tends to overclose. This overclosure can lead to a sunken appearance of the cheeks and the formation of wrinkle lines at the corners of the mouth. The anterior teeth, when present, support the lips and contribute to certain aesthetic features, such as an acute nasolabial angle. Aging, which often coincides with edentulism, exacerbates these changes due to the loss of muscle tone and skin elasticity. The tongue, being a dynamic group of muscles, tends to expand into the available space in the absence of teeth, making it initially challenging to fabricate complete or partial dentures. However, once prosthetic teeth are introduced, the tongue adapts and returns to a narrower shape. The vertical dimension of occlusion refers to the jaw relationship at the point of maximal closure when teeth are present. Tooth loss reduces this vertical dimension, allowing the mouth to overclose as the mandible moves closer to the maxilla. This overclosure contributes to the sunken appearance of the cheeks, as there is excess cheek tissue relative to the reduced vertical space. If left untreated for years, the muscles and tendons of the mandible and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) may undergo changes in tone and elasticity. Teeth are also essential for proper speech. Certain sounds in the English language, such as s, z, x, d, n, l, j, t, th, ch, and sh, require tongue-to-tooth contact for correct pronunciation. Similarly, the fricative sounds f and v rely on lip-to-tooth contact. Edentulous individuals often struggle to enunciate these sounds properly. The alveolar ridges, which are columns of bone surrounding and anchoring the teeth, run along the maxillary and mandibular dental arches. These ridges exist to support the teeth, and in their absence, the bone gradually resorbs. The maxilla resorbs in a superioposterior direction, while the mandible resorbs in an inferioanterior direction, eventually altering the individual's occlusal scheme from Class I to Class III. Additionally, the alveolus resorbs in a faciolingual direction, reducing the ridge's width. Over time, what begins as a tall, broad ridge becomes a short, narrow, and less defined structure. Resorption is accelerated by pressure on the bone, meaning long-term denture wearers experience more pronounced ridge changes than non-denture wearers. Retaining some tooth roots as overdenture abutments or placing implants can help mitigate bone loss. However, the changes described above often take many years of denture wear to develop. Ridge resorption can also lead to unpredictable ridge shapes, such as bulbous ridges with undercuts or sharp, knife-edged ridges, depending on various factors influencing the resorption process. Teeth significantly enhance masticatory efficiency, allowing thorough chewing of food. This increases the surface area for digestive enzymes in saliva, the stomach, and the intestines to act upon, facilitating proper digestion. Chewing also prepares food into small, easily swallowed boluses. For partially edentulous individuals, chewing can become difficult, depending on which teeth are missing. Loss of posterior teeth, in particular, can make chewing challenging, requiring individuals to cut food into smaller pieces and rely on their anterior teeth for mastication. This not only affects chewing efficiency but also impacts occlusion. Posterior teeth, in a mutually protected occlusion, protect the anterior teeth and maintain the vertical dimension of occlusion. When posterior teeth are missing, the anterior teeth bear excessive forces, leading to splaying. This can be prevented by obtaining dental prostheses, such as removable partial dentures, bridges, or implant-supported crowns, which restore a protected occlusion and improve chewing abilities. Altered eating habits due to tooth loss can lead to nutritional deficiencies, resulting in health problems ranging from mild to severe. Deficiencies in vitamins A, E, and C, as well as low levels of riboflavin and thiamin, can cause conditions such as constipation, weight loss, arthritis, and rheumatism. More serious conditions, such as heart disease, Parkinson's disease, and certain cancers, have also been linked to edentulism. Numerous studies have reported associations between edentulism and various medical conditions, including atherosclerotic vascular disease, heart failure, ischemic heart disease, and joint disease. The etiology of edentulism is multifactorial. While tooth extraction by a dentist contributes to edentulism, the primary cause of tooth loss in developed countries is periodontal disease. Even in the absence of tooth decay, the bone supporting the teeth may resorb, leading to tooth mobility and eventual loss. For example, tooth 21 (the lower left first premolar) may exhibit 50% bone loss with a distal horizontal defect and a mesial vertical defect, while tooth 22 (the lower left canine) may show approximately 30% bone loss.
